story.title: Ratko Mladic, former Bosnian Serb military leader, dies at 84
story.summary: Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb general convicted of genocide, has died at the age of 84. He was associated with the events of the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, where approximately 8,000 Muslim men and boys were reported missing. Mladic passed away while serving his sentence in detention at The Hague.

event_overview.title: About Bosnian War
event_overview.subject: Bosnian War
event_overview.summary: The Bosnian War was a 1992–1995 conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the breakup of Yugoslavia. It involved Bosnian government, Bosnian Serb and Bosnian Croat forces, caused widespread atrocities and displacement, and remains central to international-criminal proceedings and postwar political arrangements.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: Armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina ran from 1992 until the 1995 peace settlement; fighting ended on October 11, 1995, and the General Framework Agreement for Peace was signed in Paris on December 14, 1995.

facts.label: Location and context
facts.value: The war took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina following its move to independence amid Yugoslavia’s dissolution. ICTY findings describe armed conflict there from at least the country’s March 1992 declaration of independence through the Dayton agreement in November 1995.

facts.label: Peace settlement
facts.value: The Dayton Peace Agreement was initialled in Dayton, Ohio, in November 1995. Its 11 annexes addressed military arrangements, the inter-entity boundary, elections, the constitution, human rights, refugees and displaced people, and civilian implementation.

facts.label: Postwar political framework
facts.value: The Dayton settlement ended the war and established Bosnia and Herzegovina’s two-entity structure: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska.

facts.label: International criminal accountability
facts.value: The UN Security Council created the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in 1993 to prosecute serious violations of international humanitarian law committed in the former Yugoslavia since 1991. explore_lenses.label: Why does his death still matter in Bosnia?
explore_lenses.title: The verdict remains central to memory and reconciliation
explore_lenses.summary: Mladić's death ends his personal sentence but not the public disputes over the Srebrenica genocide, accountability and commemoration. UN officials and survivors emphasize that the final judicial findings remain part of the historical record.

claims.text: The UN secretary-general's office said Mladić's final convictions and the facts established by the courts form part of the historical record, and condemned genocide denial and glorification of people convicted of such crimes.
The UN secretary-general's office argues that accountability is essential to lasting peace, trust and reconciliation in the region.
Srebrenica Memorial head Emir Suljagić said Mladić's death does not change the judgments or resolve the work of preserving truth, responsibility and memory.

Victims' relatives cited by AP said it mattered that Mladić died in prison after receiving a life sentence, while Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić criticized the court for declining to release him before his death.

explore_lenses.label: How did he remain in Hague custody until death?
explore_lenses.title: A terminal-release request was denied days before he died
explore_lenses.summary: Mladić was held in the UN Detention Unit while awaiting transfer to a country to serve his life sentence. On August 20, the tribunal president denied a request for conditional early release to Serbia despite medical evidence that he was in the final phase of life.

claims.text: The Mechanism's Appeals Chamber affirmed Mladić's convictions and life sentence on June 8, 2021; the case record identifies convictions for genocide, crimes against humanity and war-law violations.
In an August 20 decision, the tribunal said he had served just over 15 years of a life sentence and had not reached its usual two-thirds eligibility threshold for early release.

His defense sought conditional release on humanitarian grounds, proposing direct transfer to a hospital or palliative-care facility in Serbia with Serbian supervision, principally to allow more continuous family presence.

The tribunal president found no indication that care available through the UN detention system, prison hospital and Dutch civilian facilities was inadequate, cruel, inhuman or incompatible with dignity.

explore_lenses.label: What official steps follow his death?
explore_lenses.title: Dutch procedures and a UN detention inquiry are underway
explore_lenses.summary: The court has ordered an inquiry into the circumstances of Mladić's death while Dutch authorities carry out their standard procedures. The inquiry concerns custody and death circumstances, not a reopening of his final criminal convictions.

claims.text: The International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals said Mladić died while hospitalized in The Hague and that Dutch authorities began standard procedures and investigations required under Dutch law.
Mechanism President Graciela Gatti Santana ordered a full inquiry and assigned Judge Iain Bonomy to investigate the circumstances of the death.
The written order directs Judge Bonomy to report findings to the Mechanism president as soon as reasonably possible.
The UN secretary-general's office says the convictions and sentence were final; therefore, the death inquiry does not alter the adjudicated findings.

story_report.summary: Ratko Mladić, the former Bosnian Serb military leader convicted of genocide and other war crimes connected to the Bosnian War, has died aged 84 while hospitalized in The Hague. His convictions included crimes tied to the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, and his life sentence had been affirmed on appeal in 2021. Dutch authorities began legally required procedures following his death, while the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals ordered a full inquiry into the circumstances. The final judgments and sentence remain unchanged.

sections.heading: Mladić Convictions and Life Sentence
sections.body: The Mechanism’s Appeals Chamber affirmed Mladić’s convictions and life sentence on June 8, 2021. The case record identifies convictions for genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war. An August 20 tribunal decision said he had served just over 15 years of his life term and had not met the body’s usual two-thirds threshold for early-release eligibility.

sections.heading: Mladić Release Request Drew Criticism
sections.body: Mladić’s defense had sought conditional humanitarian release, proposing transfer to a Serbian hospital or palliative-care facility under Serbian supervision, principally to allow more continuous family presence. The tribunal president found no evidence that treatment available through the UN detention system, prison hospital and Dutch civilian facilities was inadequate, cruel, inhuman or incompatible with dignity. Victims’ relatives said it mattered that he died in prison, while Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić criticized the court’s refusal to release him before his death.

sections.heading: UN and Memorial Defend Historical Record
sections.body: The UN secretary-general’s office said the final convictions and court-established facts form part of the historical record, condemning genocide denial and glorification of people convicted of such crimes. It said accountability is essential to lasting peace, trust and reconciliation in the region. Emir Suljagić, head of the Srebrenica Memorial, said Mladić’s death did not change the judgments or end the work of preserving truth, responsibility and memory.

unresolved.text: No public timetable or findings had been announced as of August 28, 2026, for either Dutch procedures or the Mechanism’s inquiry into Mladić’s death.
The immediate effect of Mladić’s death on local political tensions and genocide denial cannot yet be measured.
